title: Krishna Visits Shrutadeva and Bahulashva
story:
Two men in Mithila were preparing to receive the same guest, and neither had the faintest idea that the other was preparing as well.

Krishna was traveling through the land with a company of sages, and word of his coming ran ahead of him like a wind. Mithila had long been famous for its wise kings and its courteous people, who boasted that no guest was ever turned away hungry from its gates; that year its hospitality was about to be tested as it never had been. The news reached two houses. One was the home of Shrutadeva, a brahmana who had spent his life in study and worship, whose whole wealth was his learning and his faith. The other was the palace of Bahulashva, king of Mithila, who ruled from a hall of pillars and whose storehouses could have bought half a kingdom. The two men had nothing in common but this: each heard that the world-teacher was coming, and each took it for granted that the visit was meant for him alone.

To Shrutadeva it seemed clear that the guest of honor would honor a house of prayer. To Bahulashva it seemed equally clear that a king's palace was where such a guest belonged. Each prepared with all his household — the brahmana swept his courtyard and set out his best food; the king hung garlands in his hall and called for musicians. Each invited Krishna and the sages to stay, and neither thought to ask who else might have invited them too.

Krishna understood both hearts, and he wished to please both. He came into Mithila with the sages, and the people of the city poured out to see him pass. The king, seeing the travelers approach his gates — weary from the long road — went out to meet them, his heart overflowing, his eyes blurred with tears. With his whole family he bowed low and worshipped Krishna and the sages. Then he spoke the words of a man who can hardly believe his fortune: "Your own promise is being kept — let our eyes rest on you. Who would ever turn away from your lotus feet? You who came down into the line of Yadu for the sake of mortals wandering through the world — stay in our house for a few days, you and the brahmanas with you."

And in that same hour, across the city, the same guest was seated in the brahmana's house. Shrutadeva had spread his simple mat, set before the Lord whatever his home possessed, and bowed and worshipped with the same overflowing joy. His hands had trembled as he laid out the meal; he had rehearsed his welcome for days, and the words had failed him — and it had not mattered, because the Lord accepted what was offered and was pleased. Krishna was whole in both houses at once — fully present in the palace hall, fully present in the thatched room — and neither host saw the other, and neither host knew. In one house the guests were fed at a king's table; in the other, at a brahmana's hearth; and both tables served the same Lord.

Night fell on Mithila. Two lamps burned — one beneath the pillars of the palace, one on the mud wall of the brahmana's room — and beneath each lamp sat the same Lord, and each host's heart was full to the brim. The king slept that night as he had not slept in years; the brahmana slept the same.

Neither man ever learned the truth. Perhaps that too was grace: each received the whole of Krishna, and neither one's joy was less because another's was equal. When morning came, both houses rose blessed — each family telling the story of the night, each believing it had been the only one, and neither household ever knowing that across the city, another family was telling the same story to the same God.
reflection: Krishna honors the brahmana's hermitage and the king's palace with the same complete presence, and the wonder of the episode is that neither man's joy costs the other anything. Devotion is not measured by station, and grace is not rationed: the same Lord sits whole in a palace hall and in a thatched room, and each host receives all of him.
next_story_tease: Back in Dwaraka, however, a grief was gathering at the palace gate that no courtly joy could answer.
hero_scene: Night over Mithila: in the lamplit hall of King Bahulashva's palace, the king and his family bow low before Krishna, seated among the sages with tear-filled eyes — while across the city, in the brahmana Shrutadeva's thatched room, the same Krishna is visible seated on a simple mat, receiving the brahmana's offering under a second lamp.
